note: X posts for the agentwright-cron worker. Each item is posted once at or after `at` (within 3 hours; later than that it is skipped and reported). The worker runs at :07 every hour, so the real posting time is the first :07 at or after `at` (`at` 02:30 goes out at 03:07). No post may really go out between 03:00 and 07:00 KST, so never set `at` between 02:08 and 06:07 KST; night slots are 23:00, 01:00 and 02:00 KST, one item per slot (two items due in the same hour go out an hour apart). No links unless the item is a click-now item (max 1 link post/day). Edit on main; no redeploy needed. Before merging a change to this file run `npm run check:queues` (real posting times, length limits, links to posts that are not open yet). Optional per item: community_id (numeric X Community id the account has joined; posted with share_with_followers, falls back to a normal post + alert if refused; max 1 post per community per KST day, never the same text in two communities). Top-level "paused": true stops all posting (emergency stop for policy changes).

In a typical Claude Sonnet 5.5 request (4,000 tokens in, 600 out, 60% cached), output is 13% of the tokens and 64% of the cost.

If you want to cut your bill, look at max_tokens and answer length before you look at the prompt.

Claude Fable 5.2 costs $8 in / $40 out per million tokens, 2x Opus 5.5.

4,000 tokens in, 600 out, 60% cached:
Sonnet 5.5: $0.0094
Opus 5.5: $0.0189
Fable 5.2: $0.0373

Cache reads are $0.20/M on both Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5, so cache-heavy agents pay less than 2x.

Same request on Claude Sonnet 5.5, 4,000 tokens in and 600 out:

0% cache hits: $0.0140
60% cache hits: $0.0094

One cache_control line on the system prompt. It is the first thing to check before any pricing change.

A $20/month AI plan on Claude Sonnet 5.5, 300 requests per user: 76% margin.

The same user at 10x usage: -52%. Break-even is about 1,900 requests a month.

Run your own numbers in our free margin calculator (link in profile, under Tools).

If you recompute last month's LLM costs with today's price table, your totals move.

Store the rate used on every usage row, version the price table, and keep raw token counts so a re-price is a deliberate step.

Full write-up with code on our blog, link in profile.

Agentwright Starter is on Product Hunt today: a Next.js starter kit for Claude-powered agent SaaS with per-user cost tracking.

If you build on the Claude API, we'd like to hear what a kit like this is still missing.

https://www.producthunt.com/posts/agentwright-starter

The last line of defence most AI apps forget: a monthly spend limit on the API provider's side.

It is the only limit that still works when your own metering code has a bug.

Connecting MCP servers to your own Claude agent loop: one env variable for all servers, stdio and HTTP, namespaced tool names, an allowlist.

Plus the detail that costs money: keep tool order stable or your prompt cache misses.

On our blog, link in profile.

How our blog publishes every day without a daily deploy: each post is uploaded ahead of time, and a small Cloudflare Pages middleware returns 404 until the post's date arrives in Asia/Seoul time.

One deploy per batch of eight posts, nothing to run each morning.

The catch with Claude prompt caching: the default cache lasts 5 minutes.

10,000-token prefix on Sonnet 5.5:
5-min write $0.025
1-hour write $0.04
read $0.001

One pause over 5 minutes and you write twice: $0.05. With the 1-hour cache: $0.041. Slow users need the 1-hour one.

We made a free remote MCP server for Claude API pricing.

Add https://agentwright.app/mcp to Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor and ask "what does this workload cost on Sonnet vs Haiku?" It knows caching and Batch API prices.

No sign-up, no key. Source is public.

Our Claude starter kit's agent loop is now public in full: 104 lines of TypeScript.

Streaming, parallel tool calls, a 12-turn limit, one cache breakpoint on the system prompt, and a plan-cap check before every model turn.

Read it before you write your own. Link in profile.

Not every Claude call has a user waiting: nightly digests, tagging, evals, backfills.

Send those through the Message Batches API and they cost half the standard price. Most batches finish within an hour; requests not done in 24 hours expire.

We ran our Polar billing code in Polar's sandbox with real signed webhooks. The purchase events arrived out of order: subscription.updated before subscription.created.

The plan stayed right: an older event never overwrites a newer one, and every delivery recomputes the plan.

A 2M-token monthly cap can cost you $0.20 (all cache reads on Sonnet) or $40 (all output on Opus).

Cap each user's spend in dollars, not tokens, and reserve the worst case before the request so two parallel calls can't slip past.

Code on our blog, link in profile.

Reading the same 20,000 tokens of context on Opus 5.5:

uncached: $0.08
from cache: $0.004

That 20x gap is why how you split work between agents shows up on the bill. A helper that shares the main agent's exact prefix pays the cache price. One with its own prompt starts cold.

Each usage row in our Claude kit stores raw token counts, the cost in integer micro-dollars and the price row id.

Haiku 5.5, 3,000 tokens in, 400 tokens out: 500 micro-dollars ($0.0005).

A price change is a new row. Past totals don't move, and every charge can be explained.

A SaaS boilerplate gives you sign-in, payments and a landing page.

A product where an agent does the work needs more, because every request costs you money:

- a tool loop with a turn limit
- a usage row per model call, per user
- plan caps checked before the call
- evals in CI

Three days of posting from a brand-new X account that started with 0 followers. Real numbers:

7 timeline posts: 9 impressions each on average
2 posts in X Communities: 46 and 13
Likes: 0

Small numbers, but communities are how a new account gets read by non-followers.

We opened sales for Agentwright Starter this week: the Next.js codebase behind the posts on this account, with metering, billing, auth and the agent loop already wired.

If you build on the Claude API, we'd like to hear what a kit like this is still missing. Link in profile.

A Claude agent loop sends its prefix again on every turn. 8,000 tokens of system prompt and tools, 10 turns on Sonnet 5.5:

no cache: $0.16
with cache: $0.027 (one write, nine reads)

That is the prefix alone. Put the cache breakpoint after the tools and keep their order fixed.

Per-user cost tracking for a Claude agent is less code than it sounds.

Every API response reports four token counts: input, output, cache write, cache read. Store one row per model call with the user id, the model and those four numbers.

Cost is then four multiplications.

10,000 document summaries, 2,000 tokens in and 300 out each:

Sonnet 5.5: $70
Sonnet 5.5, Batch API: $35
Haiku 5.5: $3.50
Haiku 5.5, Batch API: $1.75

For background work the model choice moves the bill 20x. Batching then halves what is left.

Claude Haiku 5.5 bills a prompt over 100,000 tokens at long-prompt prices, for the whole request.

99,000 tokens in, 1,000 out: $0.0104
101,000 tokens in, 1,000 out: $0.053

2% more context, 5x the cost. If your retrieval step can overshoot, cap it below the line.

Before a Claude call, reserve the worst case against the user's budget: max_tokens times the output price.

max_tokens 4,096:
Opus 5.5: $0.082
Sonnet 5.5: $0.041
Haiku 5.5: $0.002

Settle to real usage after the response. Lower max_tokens, more parallel calls under a cap.

How our posts go out at night with nobody awake: a JSON queue in the repo and a Cloudflare cron Worker that runs at :07 every hour and posts the next due item, one per run.

Before any queue change, a script checks real posting times, length, quiet hours and links.

Selling an agent by usage? Find the cost floor of one task first.

Sonnet 5.5, 6 turns, 30,000 input tokens in total with 80% read from cache, 3,000 output tokens:

input $0.012
cache reads $0.0024
output $0.03

About $0.044 a task. At $0.10 a task the margin is 56%.

A turn limit is also a spend limit.

Worst case for the output of one agent run, 12 turns at max_tokens 4,096:

Opus 5.5: $0.98
Sonnet 5.5: $0.49
Haiku 5.5: $0.025

Without a turn limit a run has no worst case, and nothing to check against a user's budget before it starts.

Every turn of an agent conversation sends the whole history again.

Opus 5.5, input per turn:
400,000 tokens: $1.60, or $0.08 read from cache
40,000 after compaction: $0.16, or $0.008 from cache

Caching cuts the price per token. Compaction cuts the tokens. You want both.

Our recent posts as a 2-follower account, by where they went:

shared into a community: 13 to 41 views each
timeline only: most got 0 to 4

With no audience yet, the timeline reaches almost nobody. So we write for the communities first and make each post useful on its own.

Magic-link sign-in breaks in a way testing won't show: corporate mail scanners open every link in the email, the token is used up, the real click fails.

The fix: link to your own page with a button, and let the button go to the real callback.

On our blog, link in profile.

A 200 from the Claude API is not always a finished answer. Check stop_reason first.

If it says max_tokens, the response was cut off, and the last tool call can be incomplete. Don't run a tool on input that was truncated; raise max_tokens or retry.

Price per token is the number people compare. Cost per finished task is the one you pay.

Opus 5.5, 20,000 tokens in, 2,000 out:
no cache: $0.12
18,000 of the input read from cache: $0.052

Same model, less than half the cost. Measure cost per task from your usage table.

A Next.js agent app on Vercel and Neon:

- pooled connection string in the app, direct string for migrations
- migrations outside the build
- enough function time for long agent turns
- functions near the database
- a DB branch per preview

On our blog, link in profile.

Several workers, one Postgres jobs table, no job taken twice: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

Add a lease (locked_until) when a worker claims a job. If the worker crashes, the lease runs out and another worker picks the job up again. No extra queue service.

Claude's token counting endpoint is free and takes the same input as a real request.

Use it to reject an oversized upload, price a large request, or route by size. Inside an agent loop, the previous response's usage is usually the better estimate.

On our blog, link in profile.

The Anthropic TypeScript SDK already retries 429, 5xx and connection errors for you, with backoff.

It cannot know whether the tool that ran before the failure already sent an email or charged a card. Store each tool result before the next model call, and never run it twice.

Our X account has 3 followers. In the past week, its 5 posts on the plain timeline got 0 views. Every one.

Its 4 posts shared into X Communities got 50, 37, 31 and 11.

On a new account the timeline reaches nobody. So from today, every post goes to a community first.

Many "model mistakes" in agents are tool definition bugs.

Before: "search", "Searches the database."
After: "search_orders", "Use for the user's own past orders. Not for product questions."

Say when to call it, not only what it does.

More on our blog, link in profile.

A 2M-token monthly cap can cost you $0.20 or $40.

All cache reads on Sonnet 5.5: $0.20
All output on Opus 5.5: $40

Same cap, 200x apart. Cap each user's spend in dollars, not tokens.

More on our blog, link in profile.

We built our kit's billing on Lemon Squeezy first. Then Lemon Squeezy told us it takes no new stores and closes in March 2027.

We made Polar the default 3 days later. It was quick because plans live in our own table; the payment provider only sends events.

10,000 document summaries, 2,000 tokens in and 300 out each:

Sonnet 5.5: $70
Haiku 5.5: $3.50
Haiku 5.5 via the Batch API: $1.75

For work nobody waits for, the model choice moves the bill 20x. Batching halves what is left.

A better system prompt won't stop prompt injection.

The danger is three things in one run:
- the agent reads private data
- it reads text someone else wrote
- it can send data out

Take one of the three away for each run, in code.

More on our blog, link in profile.

Claude Sonnet 4.5 retires from the Claude API on Nov 30; requests to it then return a 404.

In our kit the model is one env variable (AGENT_MODEL), and the agent loop refuses any model without a price row before it spends a token. Switching is one line plus one price row.

The model that costs 2x per token can be cheaper per finished task.

50 tasks, 40k in / 4k out each:
Opus 5.5: $12, 45 pass = $0.27 a pass
Sonnet 5.5: $6, 20 pass = $0.30 a pass

Pass rates here are made up. Measure yours, then divide.

Same agent task, three bills: $2.04, $0.69, $0.26.

Fable 5.2 plans in all three (20k in / 2k out). Only the 10 worker calls change model (15k in / 1.5k out each): Fable, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5.

The workers are 88% of the all-Fable bill. Test cheaper ones first.

40 tools at ~250 tokens each = 10,000 input tokens on every turn, before the user types a word.

Hypothetical 20-turn session on Sonnet 5.5: $0.40 for tool definitions alone. Cached: $0.044 (one write, 19 reads).

Keep the tool list stable so it stays cached. Drop unused tools.

Our kit stores every AI cost as an integer: micro-dollars. 1 = $0.000001.

A Haiku 5.5 call, 3,000 tokens in and 400 out, is 500.

Integers add up exactly. A month of float sums would not, and you would not know which user the missing cents belong to.

Test an agent loop without paying for a single API call.

A tool is a function: unit test it. For the loop, a fake client returns a tool_use block, then end_turn. Fast, free, repeatable.

Real-model checks go in a separate eval suite.

More on our blog, link in profile.

Turn 50 of an agent chat costs far more than turn 5, because every turn sends the whole history again.

One turn on Opus 5.5:
400k tokens: $1.60 ($0.08 from cache)
40k after compaction: $0.16 ($0.008 from cache)

Caching makes tokens cheaper. Compaction makes fewer.

Postgres row-level security can silently do nothing.

The table owner skips the policies unless you add FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. Superusers always skip them.

Connect the app as a role that does not own the tables.

More on our blog, link in profile.

When people use your SaaS through an MCP server, your product analytics go blind: no page views, no clicks, no session replay.

The tool calls are the new usage log. Record each one: user, tool, duration, result size, error.

That table shows which features people actually use.

Polar's sandbox sent us subscription.updated before subscription.created.

Webhooks arrive at least once and in no fixed order. Our rule: every event re-reads the subscription and recomputes the plan, and an older event never overwrites a newer one. The plan came out right.

Valid JSON from Claude can still be broken JSON.

Check stop_reason before you parse. max_tokens means the output was cut off. A refusal may not follow your schema.

And a valid category can still be the wrong category. Only evals catch that one.

Two parallel requests can both pass "budget left?" and overspend together.

Reserve the worst case before the call: max_tokens times the output price. 4,096 on Opus 5.5 is $0.082. Settle to real usage after.

Lower max_tokens = more parallel calls under the same cap.

Log one extra field on every Claude call: the request id.

The TypeScript SDK puts it on the returned message as _request_id.

The day one call misbehaves, it is the first thing Anthropic support asks for.

The whole agent loop in our kit is 104 lines of TypeScript.

It streams, runs tool calls in parallel, stops at 12 turns, caches the system prompt and checks the user's plan before every model turn.

We kept it short on purpose: you should be able to read where the money goes.

The Batch API is half price. The catch: results come back in any order.

Set custom_id to your own job row id and match each result by it. Never by position.

Results stay downloadable for 29 days, so a crashed collector can pick them up later.

Your first AI bill surprise will most likely be one user or one runaway loop, not your average.

Three cheap alerts from your own usage table:
- daily total vs budget
- one user far above their own normal
- spend in the last hour

The provider spend limit is the last net.

Your agent may not need a vector database yet.

Postgres full-text search: a generated tsvector column, a GIN index, websearch_to_tsquery for model-written queries.

For names, ids and exact terms, keyword search is often the better tool. Add vectors when a test set says so.

Our site has a new post every day, and search engines still send us almost no one. New domain, slow indexing.

So in the first weeks, readers come from places where people already are: X Communities, dev.to, newsletters.

SEO is the long game. Communities are this month.

Never let the model tell your tool who the user is.

If get_invoices takes user_id as an argument, one sentence hidden in an uploaded PDF can ask for someone else's.

Take the user id from the server session. The model can be fooled; your auth check can't.

One-word fix for an agent's Postgres search tool: websearch_to_tsquery instead of to_tsquery.

to_tsquery throws on bad syntax, and model-written queries will hit it. websearch_to_tsquery accepts quotes, or and a leading minus, and never throws.

A Stop button does not stop the bill.

When a user cancels a Claude stream, the tokens already processed are still charged.

Pass the abort signal to the SDK and to your tools, then record the usage anyway. Otherwise your cost table says the run was free.

Combining keyword and vector search without tuning weights: reciprocal rank fusion.

score = 1/(60 + keyword rank) + 1/(60 + vector rank)

Ranks only, so ts_rank and cosine distance never need to be comparable. One SQL query does both.

We never edit a price in our kit. A price change is a new row with a start date.

Every usage row points at the price it was billed with, so last month's totals don't move when a model gets cheaper, and every charge can still be explained.

A user uploads one 50-page PDF and asks five questions. With base64 you upload the PDF five times.

With the Files API you upload it once and send a file id. The PDF's tokens are still billed per request, so cache it too.

And store which user owns which file id.

A double click can start the same agent run twice, and you pay for both.

The client sends an idempotency key, Postgres has a unique constraint on it, and the second request replays the stored answer instead of calling Claude again.

Letting an agent send emails or charge cards? Make it ask first, in code.

Stop the loop on the gated tool call, store the pending call, show the user the exact arguments, run it once on approval, then resume with the right tool_result.

Claude's web search tool costs $10 per 1,000 searches, on top of tokens.

An agent that searches 5 times per question spends $0.05 before the first token.

Set max_uses, use domain filters, and meter searches per user like tokens.

dev.to's rules say AI-assisted posts must say so, and may not promote a business, including your own.

So our dev.to posts carry an AI note, teach one thing, and stop. No product pitch.

Read each platform's AI rules before you post. They differ a lot.

Don't edit earlier turns of an agent conversation.

It breaks the prompt cache from that point on, and with thinking blocks current models can return 400s.

Store the conversation as content blocks and only append.

Find the cost floor of one agent task before you pick a price.

Sonnet 5.5, 6 turns, 30k input tokens with 80% from cache, 3k output:
input $0.012, cache reads $0.0024, output $0.03

About $0.044. At $0.10 a task the margin is 56%.

Kill switches worth having before the first incident:

- turn off one tool
- move a route to another model
- pause one user

A config table with a short cache changes them in seconds, without a deploy.

More on our blog, link in profile.

Haiku 5.5 is 20x cheaper per token than Sonnet 5.5.

In one agent request, route the easy steps there: classify, tag, extract, check a format. Keep Sonnet for the turns that need judgment.

Then compare cost per passed task, not per call.
